passages.happening:
“Then the whole congregation of Israel left the Desert of Sin, moving from place to place as the LORD commanded. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink” (verse 1).

“So the people contended with Moses, ‘Give us water to drink.’ ‘Why do you contend with me?’ Moses replied. ‘Why do you test the LORD?’” (verse 2).

“But the people thirsted for water there, and they grumbled against Moses” (verse 3). They ask why he brought them out of Egypt, to make them, their children and their animals die of thirst.
passages.hearers:
The pattern of the last two chapters comes round again: a need, a complaint, a gift. Bitter water at Marah, no food in the Desert of Sin, and now no water at all.

Where was Rephidim? It cannot be located with certainty. If Mount Sinai was the traditional Jebel Musa in the south of the peninsula, Rephidim lay in the valleys to its northwest, and the largest oasis there, the Wadi Feiran, is often suggested.

The thirst was real. Water in the Sinai comes from scattered springs and wells that a large company with flocks could quickly drain. What turns the complaint into an offense is its form. ‘Contended’ is a word at home in a law court. The people bring a case against Moses. And they ‘test the LORD’: they demand proof of what he has already shown them, again and again.
passages.later:
The psalm warns later generations: “do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness, where your fathers tested and tried Me, though they had seen My work” (Psalm 95:8-9).

Moses later tells Israel, “Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah” (Deuteronomy 6:16). Jesus quotes that command when he is tempted in the wilderness: “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7).
passages.asks: The people had seen God's power again and again, and still demanded proof. Ask whether you keep asking God to prove himself, when he has already shown you his care. And ask what it would look like to bring your real needs to him without putting him on trial.

passages.happening:
“Then Moses cried out to the LORD, ‘What should I do with these people? A little more and they will stone me!’” (verse 4).

God tells him to go ahead with some elders and his staff. “Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink” (verse 6). Moses does it in the sight of the elders.

“He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Stoning was execution carried out by the whole community. Moses' fear means the camp is turning on its leader.

God sends Moses ahead with ‘the staff with which you struck the Nile’. The staff that brought judgment on Egypt now brings water for Israel.

‘I will stand there before you by the rock.’ God himself stands at the rock. Horeb is the name Deuteronomy usually gives to Sinai, which suggests the camp was already near the mountain of God.

The place gets two names. Massah means testing. Meribah means quarreling. And the question at the heart of it all is this: ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’ They have seen the plagues, the sea, the manna and the cloud, and they still ask. The answer is water from a rock.
passages.later:
Paul reads this chapter in 1 Corinthians 10. The wilderness generation, he says, “drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). He is usually read as meaning not that the stone at Horeb was Jesus, but that the Lord who gave Israel water in the desert is the Lord now known in Christ. Then he warns the church: “We should not test Christ, as some of them did” (1 Corinthians 10:9).

Jesus offers living water: “whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst” (John 4:14). And Hebrews presses the warning of Massah on Christian readers: “do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness” (Hebrews 3:8).
passages.asks: ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’ Ask whether that has been your question in a dry season. And ask what signs of God's presence you may have missed because you were looking for proof on your own terms.

passages.happening:
“After this, the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim” (verse 8).

Moses tells Joshua to choose men and fight. “Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand” (verse 9).

“As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed” (verse 11). “When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down” (verse 12).

“So Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his army with the sword” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Now the pattern breaks. Not hunger or thirst this time, but an armed enemy.

The Amalekites were a desert people of the Negev and the Sinai. Genesis traces them to a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:12), which makes them distant relatives of Israel. They are not clearly known outside the Bible, which is not surprising for a people who left no cities or inscriptions.

Joshua appears here for the first time, as a field commander. He will lead Israel into Canaan after Moses' death.

The staff in Moses' hand is held up where the fighters below can see it. The scene does not present Moses' arms as a magic charm. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching put together around AD 200, already asked whether Moses' hands won or lost the battle. It answered that Israel prevailed whenever the people looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven.

And Moses cannot do it alone. His arms grow heavy. Aaron and Hur hold them up, one on each side. Verse 12 calls his hands ‘steady’, the Hebrew word elsewhere translated ‘faithfulness’. They stay steady because others hold them.
passages.later:
Joshua's name in Greek is the same name as Jesus. Hebrews compares the two leaders: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8).

Some early Christian writers, such as Justin Martyr, saw Moses' outstretched arms as a picture of the cross. That is a later devotional reading, not the text's own claim.

Paul asks the church to pray for one another in their struggles (Romans 15:30), as Aaron and Hur held up Moses' hands.
passages.asks: Moses' arms grew heavy, and others held them up. Ask whose arms you could hold up this week: a pastor, a parent, a friend who is worn out. And ask whether you have let anyone hold up yours.

passages.t: Written on a scroll, and an altar
passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua, because I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven’” (verse 14).

“And Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner” (verse 15).

“‘Indeed,’ he said, ‘a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation’” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time in the Bible that anyone is told to write something down. The book itself says Moses wrote this record.

The altar's name uses the word for a signal pole, raised on a hill to rally troops. ‘The LORD Is My Banner.’ The victory belongs to God, not to Joshua's sword or Moses' arms.

Verse 16 is a short, hard poetic oath. One of its words, translated ‘throne’, appears only here. Many scholars think it is a variant or a copying slip for the word ‘banner’; others keep ‘throne’, as the BSB does.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy gives the reason for the oath: “Remember what the Amalekites did to you along your way from Egypt, how they met you” when they were “tired and weary, and they attacked all your stragglers; they had no fear of God” (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). The same Law commands, “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34).

The war with Amalek comes back in 1 Samuel 15, where Saul is sent against them.
passages.hard:
Why does God swear to blot out the memory of Amalek and to war against them from generation to generation? This oath, repeated in Deuteronomy 25:17-19, lies behind the command in 1 Samuel 15 to destroy the Amalekites, and it is among the hardest words in the five books of Moses.

The text gives its reason. Amalek attacked a people just out of slavery, and Deuteronomy adds that they struck the weary stragglers at the rear and had no fear of God. Those who defend the justice of the oath stress that it is God's judgment on one people for a specific and repeated cruelty, not permission for Israel to despise foreigners, since the same law commands love for the stranger. Others read it within the customs of ancient warfare, where total destruction was a common boast: the Moabite king Mesha, around 840 BC, claimed that Israel had perished for ever. And they note that Amalekites appear alive in later stories.

Jewish tradition came to use the name Amalek for the persistent enemy of God's people, and Christians have generally read the war in light of Christ's command to love enemies. On each of these readings, the war belongs to God and not to Israel's appetite for revenge. That is what the altar's name confesses. These notes do not choose between them. One thing must be said plainly: no people living today is Amalek, and this passage gives no one permission to hate or harm any people.
passages.asks: The altar's name gives the victory to God: ‘The LORD Is My Banner’. Ask whether you are tempted to take credit for what God has done. And ask whether there is any group of people you have written off as enemies, and what Christ's command to love enemies asks of you.
